scenarios.title: Grid down (power outage, days+)
scenarios.summary: First 24 hours when the power is out and may stay out.

items.text: Check on household members, neighbours with medical needs, and anyone on powered equipment (oxygen, CPAP).
Unplug sensitive electronics; leave one lamp switched on so you notice restoration.
Keep fridge and freezer closed: a full freezer holds about 48 hours, half-full about 24. Group food together.
items.query: food safety power outage refrigerator freezer hours

items.text: Never run a generator, grill or camp stove indoors or in a garage — carbon monoxide kills silently.
Fill bathtubs and containers with water while pressure lasts; pumps may stop.
items.query: emergency water storage per person per day

items.text: Set up a single warm (or cool) room; insulate windows with blankets; layer clothing.
Charge phones from the car (engine outside, exhaust clear) and switch to battery-saver.
Tune a battery or hand-crank radio to NOAA Weather Radio (162.400–162.550 MHz) for official updates.
Food above 4 °C (40 °F) for more than 2 hours: discard. When in doubt, throw it out.
items.query: when to discard refrigerated food temperature

items.text: Carbon monoxide symptoms: headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion — get everyone outside.

scenarios.title: No safe water
scenarios.summary: Boil-water notice, failed well, or no mains supply.

items.text: Boil: rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 2,000 m / 6,500 ft). Let cool; improve taste by pouring between containers.
If you cannot boil: unscented household bleach (5–9 %): 8 drops (about 1/8 teaspoon) per gallon of clear water; double for cloudy water; stir and wait 30 minutes. Faint chlorine smell expected.
items.query: bleach drops per gallon disinfect water

items.text: Filter cloudy water through cloth or a coffee filter first; a 0.2-micron filter removes bacteria and protozoa but not viruses.
items.query: water filter viruses bacteria protozoa micron

items.text: Water heater tank and toilet tanks (not bowls) are emergency sources; avoid water near latrines or downstream of livestock.
Plan at least 1 gallon (4 litres) per person per day: half for drinking, half for hygiene. More in heat, for children, nursing mothers and the sick.
items.query: gallon per person per day water storage

items.text: Diarrhoea and vomiting: start oral rehydration early — clean water with 6 level teaspoons sugar and ½ level teaspoon salt per litre.
items.query: oral rehydration solution sugar salt litre

scenarios.title: Wildfire nearby
scenarios.summary: Smoke, evacuation warnings, or flames within sight.

items.text: If told to evacuate, go immediately. Roads close fast and smoke blinds. Do not wait for flames.
Grab the go-bag, medications, documents, pets. Wear long sleeves, closed shoes, an N95 if you have one.
Before leaving: close windows and doors, shut off gas at the meter, leave lights on, move propane tanks away from the house.
items.query: prepare home before wildfire evacuation shut off gas

items.text: In a vehicle: park away from vegetation, close windows and vents, lie on the floor under a blanket, engine running, lights on.
Smoke exposure: stay low, breathe through a damp cloth, get into a closed room with filtered air if sheltering.

scenarios.title: Hurricane or severe storm
scenarios.summary: From the watch through the first day after landfall.

items.text: Know your evacuation zone and route. Leave if ordered or if you live in a mobile home or flood zone.
Water: 1 gallon per person per day for at least 3 days; fill the bathtub for flushing and washing.
Fuel vehicles, charge everything, withdraw cash, freeze water bottles to keep food cold and as drinking water later.
Stay in an interior room away from windows; the lull in the middle may be the eye — the storm returns from the other side.
Never walk or drive through flood water: 15 cm (6 in) of moving water knocks you down, 60 cm (2 ft) floats a car.
items.query: flood water depth car float turn around

items.text: Treat all downed lines as live. Avoid standing water that may hide lines, sewage or debris.
Do not drink tap water until authorities say it is safe; see the No safe water card.

scenarios.title: Earthquake
scenarios.summary: During the shaking and the hours after.

items.text: Drop, Cover, Hold On. Under a sturdy table if possible; protect head and neck. Do not run outside while shaking.
In bed: stay there, cover your head with a pillow. Outdoors: move away from buildings, trees and lines.
Expect aftershocks. Check for injuries, then gas leaks (smell, hissing): shut off the gas only if you suspect a leak, and do not turn it back on yourself.
items.query: earthquake gas leak shut off valve

items.text: Check water lines and chimneys; put on sturdy shoes — broken glass is the most common injury.
items.query: earthquake after check damage shoes glass

items.text: Near the coast and the quake was long or strong: move inland or uphill immediately for tsunami risk.

scenarios.title: Severe bleeding
scenarios.summary: Life-threatening bleeding from a limb or trunk wound. Read the cited manual while acting.

items.text: Call for help if any service exists. Expose the wound. Apply firm, direct pressure with a clean dressing using both hands; do not let up to check.
Limb bleeding that direct pressure cannot stop: tourniquet 5–8 cm (2–3 in) above the wound, not over a joint, tightened until bleeding stops. Write the time on it. Never loosen it in the field.
Trunk, neck or groin wounds: pack the wound with gauze or clean cloth and hold firm pressure.
Treat for shock: lie the person down, keep them warm, raise legs if no spinal or leg injury, nothing by mouth.
Watch for pale, cold, clammy skin, fast weak pulse, confusion — shock is worsening; evacuate if at all possible.
items.query: signs of shock pulse skin confusion

scenarios.title: Hypothermia and cold exposure
scenarios.summary: Someone is cold, shivering or confused after exposure.

items.text: Get out of wind and wet. Remove wet clothing, insulate from the ground, cover head and neck.
items.query: hypothermia remove wet clothing insulate ground

items.text: Warm the trunk first with dry blankets and body heat; warm sweet drinks only if the person is fully alert. No alcohol.
items.query: hypothermia rewarming trunk warm drinks alcohol

items.text: Severe (no shivering, confused, drowsy): handle gently and horizontally, rough movement can stop the heart. Get medical help.
Do not rub. Rewarm in water around 37–39 °C (98–102 °F) only if there is no chance of refreezing; protect blisters.
items.query: frostbite rewarm water temperature do not rub

scenarios.title: Nuclear or radiological event
scenarios.summary: Detonation or fallout warning. Time, distance, shielding.

items.text: Get inside the most robust building you can reach within minutes; go to a basement or the centre of a large building, away from roof and outer walls.
items.query: nuclear fallout shelter get inside basement

items.text: Remove outer clothing (removes up to 90 % of contamination), bag it, shower or wipe exposed skin; do not scrub or use conditioner.
Stay inside at least 24 hours unless told otherwise; fallout radiation drops sharply in the first day. Use stored water and sealed food.
items.query: fallout stay inside 24 hours radiation decay

items.text: Potassium iodide protects only the thyroid and only from radioactive iodine; take it only when authorities advise.
items.query: potassium iodide when to take authorities

scenarios.title: Go-bag and 72-hour kit
scenarios.summary: What to have ready to leave in ten minutes.

items.text: Water (1 gallon/day for 3 days) or a filter plus bottles; 3 days of no-cook food; manual can opener.
items.query: emergency supply kit water food three days

items.text: Medications for 7 days, copies of prescriptions, glasses, first-aid kit, N95 masks, hand sanitiser.
items.query: emergency kit medications prescriptions first aid

items.text: Flashlight, battery/crank radio (NOAA), spare batteries, power bank, whistle, multi-tool, duct tape, local paper maps.
items.query: emergency kit flashlight radio whistle maps

items.text: Documents on paper and on an encrypted drive: ID, insurance, bank, medical, pet records, photos of the house contents. Cash in small bills.
Warm layer, rain shell, sturdy shoes, blanket, change of clothes; infant and pet supplies if needed.
items.query: emergency kit clothing blanket infant pet
